title: Alphabets, Scrolls and the First Books
summary: Egyptians made long rolls from a river reed called papyrus, and miners in the desert invented a short list of letters called an alphabet. Later, people wrote on animal skins, filled a giant library in Alexandria, and finally folded pages together into the very first books with covers.

sections.heading: A Reed That Became a Roll
paragraphs: Picture the banks of the Nile River in ancient Egypt about 5,000 years ago. Thick green stands of a tall water plant sway in the breeze, their stems taller than a grown-up, each topped with a fluffy, firework-shaped head. This plant is papyrus, and Egyptians found a use for almost every part of it. They ate its roots, twisted its fibres into rope, wove it into mats, baskets and sandals, and tied bundles of stems together to make light boats. But its most famous use was as a writing surface.

Here is how papyrus sheets were made. Workers cut the triangular green stems and peeled off the tough outer skin, revealing a soft, white, spongy core called the pith. They sliced the pith into long thin strips. Then they laid a row of strips side by side, all running the same direction, and placed a second layer on top running crosswise, like a lattice. The sheet was pressed or beaten with a mallet and left to dry in the sun. The plant's own sticky juices helped glue the layers together, and the result was a light, smooth, cream-coloured sheet that could be polished with a stone or shell.

It is important to know that papyrus is not true paper, even though the English word paper comes from the word papyrus. True paper, which we will meet in China in the next part of our story, is made by breaking plant fibres apart in water until they become a mushy pulp and then letting them dry into a sheet. Papyrus is different: it is made from whole strips of plant laid on top of each other, more like a very thin plywood made of reed.

Single sheets were useful, but Egyptians wanted longer surfaces. So they glued sheets edge to edge to make a roll, often around twenty sheets long as a standard size. Rolls could be joined to make even longer ones. Writers usually wrote first on the side where the fibres ran horizontally, because the pen moved more smoothly along the grain. A famous Egyptian medical text called the Ebers Papyrus, from around 1550 BCE, fills a roll about 20 metres long, longer than a tennis court.

Papyrus was in use in Egypt by about 3000 BCE. One of the oldest rolls ever found, discovered in the tomb of an official named Hemaka at Saqqara and dating from around that time, is said to have been completely blank, perhaps as if it had been packed for writing in the afterlife. Scribes wrote on it with reed brushes and black and red ink. Over the centuries Egypt became the world's supplier of papyrus, exporting it across the Mediterranean. The Greeks and then the Romans used it for letters, contracts, poems and history books. A Greek book was really a roll, and long works were divided into several rolls, which is why ancient texts are still split into 'books' today.

Papyrus was a giant step up from clay. It was light, easy to carry, and could be rolled up and stored on a shelf or in a jar. But it had weaknesses too. In damp climates it slowly rots and crumbles, which is why most surviving ancient papyri come from the hot, dry sands of Egypt. It could tear along the fibres, it was hard to fold without cracking, and because it grew mainly in Egypt, everyone else depended on the Egyptian supply. Papyrus was too expensive for many uses, so even Egyptian students did their homework on broken pottery.

sections.heading: Miners, Ox Heads and the First Letters
paragraphs: Papyrus made writing lighter. The next great invention made writing simpler. To understand why it mattered, remember the problem from Part 1: cuneiform needed hundreds of signs, and Egyptian hieroglyphs needed hundreds more. Learning them took years, so only a small group of professional scribes could read. What if you could write every word in a language using only a couple of dozen signs?

That is exactly what an alphabet does. An alphabet uses a small set of letters, each standing for one basic sound. Mix and match those letters and you can spell any word, even a word nobody has ever written before. Today the English alphabet has 26 letters, and a five-year-old can learn them all.

The story of the alphabet begins, surprisingly, in Egypt, among people who were not Egyptian. In the winter of 1904 to 1905 the British archaeologist Flinders Petrie and his wife Hilda were exploring Serabit el-Khadim, a remote spot in the mountains of the Sinai Peninsula where ancient Egyptians mined turquoise. Near a temple to the goddess Hathor, they found short inscriptions scratched into rocks and small statues. The signs looked a bit like hieroglyphs, but there were only a few dozen of them, and they were used in an unfamiliar way.

In 1916 the Egyptologist Alan Gardiner worked out the trick. The writers had borrowed pictures from Egyptian writing but used each picture for the first sound of its name in their own Semitic language. The picture of an ox head was called alp, meaning ox, so it stood for the sound at the start of that word. The picture of a house was called bayt, meaning house, so it stood for the sound b. This idea, where a letter gets its sound from the first sound of the thing it pictures, is called the acrophonic principle. Gardiner read one repeated group of signs as 'to the Lady', probably meaning the goddess worshipped at the mine.

Scholars call this early alphabet Proto-Sinaitic. Many of the Sinai inscriptions are thought to date to roughly the 1700s or 1600s BCE, though some researchers argue for around 1800 BCE. Then, in the 1990s, two short inscriptions were found carved on a cliff at Wadi el-Hol, a desert valley in Middle Egypt, dated to roughly 1900 to 1800 BCE. These suggest that the alphabet was born among Semitic-speaking workers, soldiers or traders living in or around Egypt, who adapted Egyptian picture-signs into a far simpler system.

The beautiful part of this story is that the alphabet was probably not invented by elite scribes in a palace, but by ordinary people who needed a practical way to write. They kept just one sign per consonant sound, so the whole system needed only around two dozen signs.

Over the following centuries, these letters spread northward along the trade routes of Canaan, the land along the eastern Mediterranean coast. Different groups wrote them in slightly different ways. Slowly, the letters became simpler lines rather than recognisable pictures. The ox head was turned on its side and became a simple shape that, many centuries later, would be flipped again and become our capital A. If you turn an A upside down, you can still imagine the horns of an ox.

sections.heading: Twenty-Two Letters for the Sea Traders
paragraphs: By around 1050 BCE, one version of this alphabet had become standard in the busy port cities of Phoenicia, along the coast of what is now Lebanon. The Phoenicians were the great sea traders of the ancient Mediterranean. From cities such as Byblos, Tyre and Sidon, they sailed far and wide, selling cedar wood, glass and a famous purple dye made from sea snails, and they founded colonies such as Carthage in North Africa.

The Phoenician alphabet had 22 letters, all of them consonants. There were no letters for vowels at all, so readers had to fill in the vowel sounds from context, a bit like reading 'txt msgs' where you can usually guess 'text messages'. It was written from right to left. One of the most famous early Phoenician inscriptions is carved on the stone coffin of a king named Ahiram of Byblos, dated to around 1000 BCE, warning anyone who disturbs his tomb that they will be punished.

For merchants, this alphabet was perfect. A trader did not need years of scribal school. He could learn 22 letters quickly and use them to keep accounts, write contracts and send messages to partners in faraway ports. Because Phoenician ships visited so many places, their alphabet travelled too. It became the ancestor of an astonishing number of scripts. Through Aramaic, a related script used across the Persian Empire, it led to the Hebrew and Arabic scripts. And when it reached the Greeks, it began the line that leads to the letters you are reading right now.

sections.heading: The Greeks Add Vowels
paragraphs: Sometime around 800 BCE, Greeks who traded with the Phoenicians borrowed their alphabet. The Greeks even admitted the borrowing: some ancient Greek writers called letters 'Phoenician things'. But Greek had a problem. The Greek language depends heavily on vowel sounds, and a script with no vowels made Greek words very hard to read.

So the Greeks made a small change with enormous consequences. Some Phoenician letters stood for consonant sounds that Greek did not use. Instead of throwing those letters away, the Greeks recycled them as vowels. The Phoenician aleph, the old ox-head letter, became alpha, the sound a. The letter he became epsilon, the sound e. Others became the vowels i, o and later u. For the first time, an alphabet had separate letters for both consonants and vowels, so a reader could sound out almost any word exactly. Many historians call this the first full alphabet.

Even the word alphabet comes from this moment: it joins the names of the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta, which came from the Phoenician aleph and bet, ox and house. So when you say 'alphabet', you are really saying 'ox-house', a little fossil of the miners of Sinai hiding inside an everyday word.

Early Greek writing went in different directions. Some inscriptions ran right to left like Phoenician. Some ran in a back-and-forth zigzag called boustrophedon, which means 'as the ox turns', like an ox ploughing a field: one line left to right, the next line right to left. Eventually Greeks settled on writing left to right, the direction used in Europe ever since.

Greek colonists carried their alphabet to southern Italy, including the city of Cumae near Naples. There the Etruscans, a powerful people of central Italy, adopted it, and the Romans learned it in turn. The Latin alphabet of classical Rome had 23 letters. Letters such as J, U and W were added much later, in the Middle Ages and after. As the Roman Empire grew, the Latin alphabet spread across western Europe. Meanwhile, more than a thousand years later, a version of the Greek alphabet became the basis of Cyrillic, used today for Russian and other languages.

Why does all of this matter for the story of printing? Because an alphabet with about two dozen letters is perfect for movable type. Much later, a European printer would need to cast many copies of only a few dozen letters, plus capitals, numbers and punctuation, rather than many thousands of different characters. The simplicity of the alphabet, invented by desert workers and improved by Greek traders, quietly prepared the ground for Gutenberg nearly 3,000 years later.

sections.heading: Writing on Skins: Parchment and Vellum
paragraphs: Papyrus grew in Egypt, but people elsewhere needed something they could make at home. One answer came from animals. Parchment is a writing material made from specially prepared animal skin, usually from sheep, goats or calves. The finest kind, made from calfskin, is called vellum. People had written on animal hides for a very long time, but parchment is something special: it is not leather, because it is not tanned. It is stretched and dried skin.

Making parchment was hard, smelly work. First the skin was soaked in water for about a day to clean it. Then it went into a bath of lime, a strong chemical made from burnt limestone, for several days, which loosened the hair. The parchment maker scraped away the hair and fat and stretched the wet skin tight on a wooden frame. While it dried under tension, he scraped it again and again with a curved, half-moon-shaped knife until it was thin, smooth and even. Rubbing it with pumice stone made a surface that ink would grip. The finished sheet was strong, pale and could be written on both sides.

The word parchment comes from the name of Pergamon, a wealthy Greek city in what is now western Turkey, which was a famous centre for making it. There is a well-known story about how this happened, told by the Roman writer Pliny the Elder in the first century CE, who said he got it from an earlier scholar named Varro. According to the tale, the kings of Egypt and the kings of Pergamon were rivals, each trying to build the greatest library. To stop Pergamon, the Egyptian king banned the export of papyrus, and so the people of Pergamon invented parchment instead. It is a great story, but it is a legend. Writing on prepared skins was known long before Pergamon became important. The most likely truth is that Pergamon became famous for making excellent parchment, so its name stuck.

Parchment had big advantages over papyrus. It was tough, it could be folded without cracking, it lasted well even in damper climates, and it could be made anywhere that had farm animals. If a scribe made a mistake, he could gently scrape the ink off with a knife and write again. People sometimes scraped whole books clean and reused the parchment for new texts. A reused page like this is called a palimpsest. Today, scientists use special lighting and imaging to read the faint older writing hidden underneath, recovering lost works, including writings by the ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes.

The big disadvantage was cost. Each animal gave only a few large sheets. A large book needed the skins of dozens or even hundreds of animals. One of the most extreme examples is the Codex Amiatinus, a giant Latin Bible made around 700 CE at the monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow in northern England. It has 1,040 leaves of vellum, weighs about 34 kilograms, heavier than many 11-year-olds, and is about 49 centimetres tall. The manuscript expert Christopher de Hamel estimated its pages used the skins of around 515 cattle, and the monastery set out to make three of these huge Bibles. Today the Codex Amiatinus is kept in a library in Florence, Italy.

Parchment would remain the main writing material of Europe for more than a thousand years, until paper arrived. In fact, it is still used today for Jewish Torah scrolls, and until 2015 the United Kingdom recorded its new laws on vellum.

sections.heading: The Great Library of Alexandria
paragraphs: Now let us visit the most famous library of the ancient world. After Alexander the Great died in 323 BCE, one of his generals, Ptolemy, took control of Egypt and founded a royal family that ruled for nearly 300 years. Their capital was Alexandria, a gleaming city on the Mediterranean coast with a giant lighthouse, the Pharos, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

Around 300 BCE the first Ptolemy, perhaps encouraged by the Greek scholar Demetrius of Phalerum (according to one ancient account), began planning a great centre of learning. It was called the Mouseion, a temple to the Muses, the goddesses of the arts and sciences. This is where our word museum comes from. His son, Ptolemy II, built up its library. The goal was breathtaking: to collect a copy of every important book in the world.

The Ptolemies were famously determined. According to ancient accounts, when ships docked in Alexandria's harbour, officials searched them for books. Any scrolls found were taken to the library and copied by hand. The library kept the originals, and the owners were given the copies. Agents travelled around the Mediterranean buying texts, and the library is said to have borrowed official copies of the great Greek plays from Athens, paying a huge deposit, and then kept the originals, happily losing its money.

How many scrolls did it hold? Ancient writers give numbers as high as 400,000 or even 700,000 scrolls, while other ancient estimates are far smaller. Modern historians think these numbers are probably exaggerated, and many scrolls held only part of a work, but it was clearly the largest collection of its time. Remember, every one of those scrolls had been copied by hand, letter by letter, with a reed pen on papyrus. Imagine teams of copyists bent over their desks day after day, checking each line.

The library was also a research centre. The scholar Callimachus created a giant catalogue of its holdings, called the Pinakes, which ran to 120 volumes by itself and is often called the first library catalogue. Eratosthenes, one of the library's head librarians, used shadows and geometry to estimate the size of the Earth surprisingly well. Scholars at Alexandria compared different copies of Homer, marked errors and tried to produce the most accurate text. That problem, how to stop mistakes creeping in when books are copied by hand, is one that only printing would truly solve.

You may have heard that the library was destroyed in one great fire, perhaps when Julius Caesar's soldiers set ships ablaze in 48 BCE. Historians now think the real story is slower and sadder. That fire probably burned warehouses near the docks, and the library continued to be mentioned afterwards. Its decline came over centuries, as royal funding dried up, scholars were driven away in 145 BCE, and wars damaged the city in the 200s CE. Knowledge can be lost not only in flames, but simply when nobody pays to look after it.

sections.heading: From Scroll to Codex
paragraphs: For most of ancient history, a book was a scroll. Scrolls worked, but they were awkward. You needed both hands to read, unrolling with one hand and rolling up with the other. If you wanted to find a passage near the end, you had to unroll almost the whole thing. Most scrolls had writing on one side only, wasting half the material. And a long work needed many scrolls, which had to be stored in boxes or on shelves with little tags hanging off the ends to show their titles.

Romans already used a different kind of writing object for notes: wooden tablets coated with wax, which they scratched with a pointed stylus and could smooth over to reuse. Two or more tablets were often tied together along one edge with cord, so they opened and closed like a book. At some point, people realised they could do the same thing with sheets of parchment or papyrus: stack them, fold them in half, and stitch them together along one side. The result was the codex, the ancestor of every book on your shelf. The word comes from the Latin caudex, meaning tree trunk or block of wood, a memory of those wooden tablets.

In the first century CE, the Roman poet Martial praised small parchment codices of famous authors, telling readers that such a book was compact enough to carry on a journey and could be held in one hand. To him it was a handy new travel format, almost like a paperback.

The codex had many advantages. Both sides of every page could be used, so it held more text for the same amount of material. Its covers protected the pages. It stacked neatly on a shelf. Most importantly, you could flip straight to any page, which made it much easier to look things up, compare passages and add page references. Early Christians seem to have liked the codex especially for their sacred writings, perhaps because it was practical for carrying and for finding passages, though historians still debate exactly why.

The change happened gradually. By around 300 CE, codices and scrolls were roughly equal in number among surviving books from Egypt, and during the 400s and 500s the codex largely replaced the scroll for books in the Roman world. One of the great surviving codices from this period is the Codex Sinaiticus, a Greek Bible handwritten on parchment in the 300s CE. By the time the Roman Empire in the west was ending, the book had taken the basic shape it still has today: pages, a spine and covers.

sections.heading: The Mystery of the Phaistos Disc
paragraphs: Before we leave the ancient world, let us look at one of its strangest puzzles. On 3 July 1908, the Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier was digging in the ruins of a Minoan palace at Phaistos on the island of Crete. In a storeroom he found a round disc of fired clay about 16 centimetres across, a little bigger than a CD. Both sides were covered with little pictures arranged in a spiral, running from the edge towards the centre.

The pictures include a walking man, a head wearing a plumed headdress, a fish, a bird, a ship, a bow and many other shapes. There are 45 different signs, used 242 times in total, divided into groups by lines. Here is what makes the disc so remarkable: the signs were not drawn or scratched by hand. Each one was pressed into the wet clay using a separate stamp, before the disc was fired. Every time the same sign appears, it looks almost exactly the same, because the same stamp made it.

That means someone, perhaps around 1700 BCE, though the date is uncertain and estimates range across several centuries, had a set of carved stamps, one for each symbol, and used them to 'type' a text into clay. It is a little like an ancient set of rubber stamps. Some people have called it the world's first printed document, or even an early form of movable type.

But we should be careful. Nobody has ever deciphered the Phaistos Disc, so we do not know what language it records, whether it is a prayer, a story or a list, or even whether it was made in Crete at all. It is the only object of its kind ever found. No other text made with the same stamps has turned up, and there is no sign of a workshop producing stamped documents. So the Phaistos Disc was a curiosity, a brilliant one-off experiment, not the start of a printing industry. Today it sits in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum on Crete, still guarding its secret.

By around 400 CE, then, the world had made huge progress. People had alphabets that were easy to learn, light rolls of papyrus, tough sheets of parchment, giant libraries and the codex, the book with pages. But every single book was still copied by hand, and the materials were costly. Scrolls and skins were expensive, but far to the east, someone was about to make a cheap new writing material from plants and rags.

deepDive: Historians love to argue about why the codex replaced the scroll. The numbers are clear enough: among surviving books from Roman Egypt, codices were a small minority in the first and second centuries CE, roughly matched scrolls by around 300 CE, and by the 400s and 500s far outnumbered them. The classic study by Colin Roberts and T. C. Skeat noticed that Christian texts from Egypt were almost always codices, even when most non-Christian literature was still copied on rolls. Some scholars think Christians chose the codex because it was cheaper, using both sides of the page; others think it was easier to search for passages during worship and debate; others suggest an early, influential Christian book was a codex and set the fashion. The truth may be a mix, and the evidence is limited mostly to what survived in Egypt's dry sands. A second debate concerns the alphabet. Older textbooks often credited the Phoenicians with inventing it, but the Sinai and Wadi el-Hol discoveries show that alphabetic writing existed hundreds of years earlier among Semitic speakers in and around Egypt, with the Phoenician version being one well-organised descendant. Linguists also argue about terms: because Phoenician had no vowel letters, many call it an abjad rather than a true alphabet, reserving alphabet for the Greek system that added vowels. Numbers about ancient libraries deserve skepticism too. Ancient authors often gave enormous rounded figures, such as 400,000 or 700,000 scrolls at Alexandria, perhaps to glorify the Ptolemies. Modern estimates are much smaller and difficult to pin down, since a single work could fill many rolls and one roll could hold several short works. Finally, the Phaistos Disc shows why historians separate an idea from an industry. The idea of stamping repeatable signs appears in seals, brick stamps and this disc, but it only changes the world when combined with cheap materials, enough demand, and a whole system of tools and workers, which is the story of the parts to come.
funFact: The word alphabet comes from alpha and beta, the first two Greek letters, which go back to old Semitic words meaning ox and house.
